newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Vietnam coffee dogged by high moisture, rain-trade.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam coffee dogged by high moisture, rain-trade.

text.p: Vietnam's new robusta harvest is being dogged by high moisture levels in the coffee beans after heavy rains and this is making drying and transportation difficult, coffee traders said on Wednesday.

"It's been raining all over the place. The moisture level in the beans reaches 20 percent when it should only be at 13 percent. That's much too high," a senior trader in a Western commodity house said.
A few thousand tonnes of coffee beans were sold in the past week, mainly from the region of Dong Nai, traders said.
But the crop from Dak Lak province, which produces two-thirds of the 240,000-270,000 tonnes of coffee beans exported by Vietnam each year, has only come in trickles to the major ports such as Saigon.
"We're getting a small quantity of beans from Dak Lak," a Singapore-based dealer said.

"The report we received from Dak Lak was that it was dry yesterday, but you need a week of dry weather to be able to dry the beans and export. They don't have enough of the machinery to dry the beans," one trader explained.
Trading in Indonesian robusta coffee was thin this week with most of the crop there already sold. "Indonesia is not competitive at the moment," one dealer said.

Prices of Vietnam's Grade 2, 80 percent black and broken, robusta beans were quoted in a range between US$1,090/$1,140 a tonne FOB Saigon port, down slightly from last week's quote of $1,120/$1,140 a tonne, traders said.
Indonesian Grade 4 robusta beans were priced at around $1,200/$1,250 a tonne FOB Panjang against $1,230/$1,300 a tonne last week, the dealers said.

LIFFE robusta coffee futures are expected to rise between $10-$20 a tonne when the market opens later in London on Wednesday, mainly on the back of higher prices overnight in New York. The most active January contract closed in London on Tuesday $12 higher at $1,401 a tonne.
"It's going to just follow New York's lead and move about $10-$20 higher," a coffee trader here said.
"But aside from New York, the market is purely range-bound and any movement will not really get far," another dealer said.
The November/January LIFFE contract spread, a key barometer of nearby supply availability, will probably remain steady, dealers said.
The spread stood at $94 at the close on Tuesday, down $31 from Monday's close.
Singapore January robusta coffee futures closed at $1,279 a tonne on Tuesday after three tonnes were traded at $1,300.
On Monday, three tonnes of the January contract settled at $1,298 a tonne and four tonnes of the March contract finished at $1,258 a tonne in quiet trade on the Singapore Commodity Exchange.
